title: Blocking others from Allah's way empties your own deeds.
subtitle: Deeds that come to nothing
then: This surah came in Madinah when the small community was hemmed in by enemies. It opens on those who rejected Allah and {trap}blocked others from His path.{/trap} Ibn Kathir says Allah makes their deeds futile and denies them any reward, {trap}like dust scattered in the air.{/trap}
now: Your friend wants to start praying and you joke about it until she stops. Your colleague wants to give charity and you talk him out of it. {trap}Getting in someone else's way is its own deed.{/trap} {idea}Be the person who opens the door, not the one who blocks it.{/idea}
old: What others do with their faith is not affected by me.
new: If I block someone from good, I lose more than they do.
try: Encourage one person today in a good thing they are trying to do.

title: He wipes away their sins and sets their affairs right.
subtitle: The surah where Muhammad ﷺ is named
then: The surah takes its name from this verse, which names Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn Kathir explains Bal as {reward}their matter, their affair, their condition.{/reward} He notes the Prophet ﷺ taught the reply to one who sneezes: {idea}may Allah guide you and set your affairs right.{/idea}
now: Your life feels tangled: the job, the debt, the family tension, the thing you keep doing that you hate. {reward}The promise here is not just a clean record but a sorted life.{/reward} Belief and good deeds are the first thread to pull.
old: Faith might clean my record, but my life stays messy.
new: Allah promises to set my whole condition right when I believe and do good.
try: When someone sneezes today and praises Allah, reply with may Allah guide you and set your affairs right.

title: The difference is what each side chose to follow.
subtitle: Falsehood or truth from their Lord
then: This verse explains the two before it. Ibn Kathir says deeds are lost for one group and sins forgiven for the other {idea}because one chose falsehood over truth, and the other followed the truth from their Lord.{/idea} Allah makes the end of each path clear.
now: Every day you pick what to follow: which voice in your feed, which friend's advice, which inner urge. {idea}It does not feel like a big decision.{/idea} But the verse says outcomes come from the thing you keep following.
old: Where people end up is mostly chance.
new: Where I end up depends on what I choose to follow, and Allah has made both paths clear.
try: List three voices you follow most. Ask of each: does this lead me to truth?

title: He could have done it Himself; He tests you through each other.
subtitle: Rules for a besieged community, and a deeper purpose
then: The surah introduction says fighting had been ordered for a tiny, boycotted Madinah facing all of Arabia. The verse gives battle guidance, including freeing captives by grace or ransom. {idea}Allah could have punished the enemy Himself, but He lets people be tested by each other.{/idea} {reward}Those killed in His cause will never have their deeds lost.{/reward}
now: The difficult manager. The relative who tests your patience every visit. You wonder why Allah does not just fix it. {idea}The verse says some of us are tested through others.{/idea} How you act in that friction is the point.
old: If Allah wanted, He would just remove the hard people from my life.
new: Allah could remove every difficulty, but some are there to test and grow me.
try: Think of one person who tests you. Choose one calm response before you see them next.

title: Guided onward and their condition set right.
subtitle: What Allah does for those who gave their lives
then: Many believers would die in the coming battles. Ibn Kathir says Allah would multiply their deeds, and that {reward}He will guide them means He will guide them to Paradise.{/reward} {idea}Their situation and affairs will be set right.{/idea}
now: You sit with a family who lost someone good: a nurse who worked through the pandemic, a father who died working to feed his kids. It looks like an ending. {reward}The verse says for those who die striving for Allah, the story keeps going.{/reward}
old: When a good person dies young, it is simply a loss.
new: For those who give themselves for Allah, death opens onto guidance and repair.
try: Make dua today for one good person you know who has passed away.

title: A Paradise He has already made known to them.
subtitle: Not a strange place, but a known one
then: This finishes the promise to those who died in Allah's cause. {reward}He admits them to Paradise, which He has made known to them.{/reward} Ibn Kathir explains it as a place Allah has acquainted them with. {idea}They arrive somewhere they recognize.{/idea}
now: Walking into your childhood home after years abroad: you know where the light switch is without looking. {reward}The verse describes Paradise like that for the believer: not a stranger's place, but one made known.{/reward}
old: Paradise is a far, unknown place I cannot picture.
new: Allah makes Paradise known to its people, so it feels like home.
try: Read one verse describing Paradise today and picture it as a home being prepared.

title: Support Allah's cause and He steadies your feet.
subtitle: Help that comes back to the helper
then: The believers in Madinah were few, poor, and surrounded, as the surah introduction describes. {idea}They are told: if you support Allah's cause, He will support you.{/idea} {reward}He will make your feet firm{/reward}, which is what a frightened, outnumbered group needs most.
now: You stand up for what is right in a meeting and your voice shakes. You keep praying through a stressful exam season. {reward}The verse says the steadiness comes after you take the step.{/reward} Your feet get firmer while you are standing.
old: I need to feel strong before I can stand up for what is right.
new: When I stand for Allah's cause, He gives me the steadiness I lacked.
try: Do one small right thing today that makes you a little nervous, and ask Allah to steady you.

title: For the rejecters, stumbling, and deeds that come to nothing.
subtitle: The opposite of firm feet
then: Right after the promise of firm feet comes its opposite. {trap}For those who disbelieve there is misery, and Allah makes their deeds vain.{/trap} The same pairing as the surah's opening: {idea}what you build on decides whether it lasts.{/idea}
now: You pour years into a goal with no thought of Allah: the house, the title, the follower count. {trap}It can all be real and still come to nothing in the end.{/trap} {idea}The same effort with Allah in it becomes something that lasts.{/idea}
old: As long as I work hard, it all adds up.
new: Effort only lasts when it is built on faith.
try: Before your main task today, say Bismillah and set an intention for Allah.

title: They hated what Allah sent, so their deeds lost their worth.
subtitle: Dislike of revelation is the root
then: The verse names the reason behind the lost deeds. {trap}They disliked what Allah sent down.{/trap} {idea}The problem began in the heart, as a feeling toward revelation, before it showed in deeds.{/idea}
now: A verse comes up that asks something hard of you: about money, or a relationship, or your tongue. {trap}You feel a small flinch of dislike.{/trap} {idea}That flinch is worth noticing gently, not hiding.{/idea} Ask Allah to make you love what He sent.
old: My feelings about a verse do not matter if I mostly obey.
new: How my heart feels toward what Allah sent shapes the worth of everything I do.
try: Think of one Quranic teaching you resist. Ask Allah to help your heart accept it.

title: Walk the land and look at how others ended.
subtitle: History as a mirror
then: The verse asks those who denied the Prophet ﷺ to travel and look. Ibn Kathir says Allah punished the earlier nations for their denial {reward}and saved the believers among them.{/reward} {trap}A similar end awaits those who repeat it.{/trap}
now: You visit a museum or ruins on holiday and take photos. {idea}The verse asks for a different kind of looking: what did these people choose, and how did it end?{/idea} Then turn the question on your own habits.
old: History is about other people and other times.
new: The end of those before me is a mirror for my own choices.
try: Next time you read or watch any history, ask one question: what does this teach me?

title: Allah is our Protector, and you have none.
subtitle: The answer given at Uhud
then: Ibn Kathir recounts that after Uhud, Abu Sufyan boasted of his idols: {trap}we have al-Uzza and you have none.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ told his companions to reply: {idea}Allah is our Protector, and you have no protector.{/idea} This verse says the same.
now: Someone mocks you: they have connections, money, a big family behind them, and you seem to have no one. {idea}Your reply does not need to be loud.{/idea} {reward}You have a Protector they cannot see.{/reward}
old: Without people or power behind me, I am unprotected.
new: Allah is the Protector of those who believe, whatever their numbers.
try: When you feel outnumbered today, say quietly: Allah is my Protector.

title: Eating like cattle, with no thought beyond the plate.
subtitle: Two ways to live, two places to end
then: Ibn Kathir says those who disbelieve {trap}eat like animals, munching with greed, with no concern beyond it.{/trap} He cites the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}a believer eats with one intestine, and a disbeliever with seven.{/idea}
now: Dinner in front of a screen, one more episode, a second plate you did not need. {trap}Life becomes intake.{/trap} {idea}The verse is not against food; it is against a life that is only about the next bite.{/idea}
old: Eating well and enjoying myself is all there is to a good life.
new: Enjoyment is fine, but a life with no aim beyond the plate is a life wasted.
try: At one meal today, eat without a screen and thank Allah before and after.

title: Stronger cities than the one that drove you out are gone.
subtitle: Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ who left Makkah
then: Ibn Abbas reported that at the cave during the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ looked back at Makkah and said {reward}you are the most beloved of Allah's lands to Allah and to me; had I not been driven out, I would never have left.{/reward} {idea}Allah then revealed that mightier towns had been destroyed, with none to help them.{/idea}
now: You had to leave a home, a job, a country, because of other people. You still miss it. {reward}The Prophet ﷺ loved the home he was forced from.{/reward} {idea}Loving a place is not weakness, and those who push you out do not have the last word.{/idea}
old: If I was pushed out, they won and my love for that place was foolish.
new: I can love what I lost and trust Allah with those who pushed me out.
try: If you miss a place you had to leave, make a short dua for it and its people.
